chunks: Magnetic current sensing pros and cons. The question: How does inductive/magnetic current sensing work? What are its pros and cons?
Magnetic current sensing reads the magnetic field that a current makes, instead of the voltage it drops across a resistor.
That gives you electrical isolation and almost no power loss. A Hall sensor reads the field directly and works for steady (DC) and alternating (AC) current.
Current transformers and Rogowski coils respond only to changing current, so they work for AC only. The price is higher cost, offset drift and poor accuracy at small currents.
Imagine feeling the wind from a fan without touching it. A Hall sensor is like a flag that leans steadily as long as the wind blows, so it reports steady wind too.
A current transformer is like a pinwheel that only spins while the wind speed is changing: a steady wind gives it nothing. Both keep your hand away from the fan.
Stray wind from other fans, meaning nearby wires and magnets, adds error to both.
Hall principle.

A bias current flows along the plate; the field from the measured conductor pushes the moving carriers sideways (Lorentz force), so a voltage appears across the plate, between the edges perpendicular to both the bias current and B.
It is proportional to B and therefore to the measured current; its sign depends on the carrier type.
Because V H depends on B itself, not on its rate of change, this works at DC, unlike induction.
Hall effect: a magnetic field pushes moving charges sideways in a thin plate, making a small voltage proportional to the field.
Current transformer (CT): the measured wire passes through a ring with an N -turn coil, which carries I p over N .
Burden resistor: the resistor across a CT's coil that turns its current into a voltage.
Rogowski coil: a coil whose output follows how fast the current changes, so a circuit must add it up over time.
A wire carrying 10 amps makes a field of B equals micro 0 I over (2 pi r) equals 0. 2 mT at 1 cm, which is tiny, so real sensors use a core or a close conductor to concentrate it.
For a CT with 1000 turns, 10 amps in the wire gives 10 over 1000 equals 10 milliamps in the coil. A 100 ohms burden turns that into 0. 01 times 100 equals 1 volts.
A steady DC current would give no output at all, because nothing is changing. That is the whole idea.
"Magnetic sensing measures the field around the conductor instead of a voltage drop. Hall sensors detect the field directly and work at DC and AC.
Current transformers and Rogowski coils use Faraday induction, so they only see AC. The big advantages are isolation, almost no insertion loss and high current range.
The downsides are cost, size, offset and temperature drift, sensitivity to stray fields, and poor accuracy at small currents compared with a shunt."
